---
title: "Recovering the depth of a cascade"
description: >
  Simulate a hierarchical cascade, read its depth and class from the
  log-cumulants of the innermost temperature, test a fixed depth, and do the
  same from the degree sequence of a network.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.2, dpi = 150, fig.align = "center")
library(htheoryR)
# Okabe-Ito palette; every curve also has its own line type or symbol
pal <- c("#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#009E73", "#CC79A7", "#E69F00", "#56B4E9")
par_default <- function() par(mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 1, 1), las = 1, bty = "l",
                              cex.axis = 0.9)
```

Every number and plot on this page is computed by `htheoryR` when the site is
built. The page runs in a few seconds.

## The cascade

A cascade of depth $N$ starts at $T_0$ and draws each temperature from a
gamma law (class $s = 1/2$) or an inverse-gamma law (class $s = 1$) whose
mean is the temperature of the level above, with shape $a_i$. Every level
keeps the mean, $\mathrm{E}[T_N] = T_0$, but adds dispersion. `sample_TN()`
draws $T_N$ directly.

```{r cascade, fig.cap = "Density of log T_N for depths N = 1, 2, 3 (class s = 1/2, a = 2, 10^5 draws each). Deeper cascades are more dispersed, with a longer left tail."}
set.seed(1)
logT <- lapply(1:3, function(N) log(sample_TN(rep(2, N), s = 0.5, size = 1e5)))
dens <- lapply(logT, density, n = 512)
par_default()
plot(NULL, xlim = c(-5, 2), ylim = c(0, max(sapply(dens, function(d) max(d$y)))),
     xlab = expression(log~T[N]), ylab = "density")
for (N in 1:3) lines(dens[[N]], col = pal[N], lwd = 2, lty = N)
legend("topleft", legend = paste("N =", 1:3), col = pal[1:3], lty = 1:3,
       lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

## Why the log-cumulants identify the depth

The cascade is multiplicative, so $\log T_N$ is a sum of $N$ independent
terms. Its cumulants of order two and higher are sums over the levels. For
equal shapes, every level contributes the same amount:

$$\kappa_r(\log T_N) = N\,\kappa_r^{(1)}(a), \qquad r \ge 2 .$$

The ratio $\rho_s(a) = \kappa_3/\kappa_2$ therefore does not depend on $N$. It
is negative for $s = 1/2$ and positive for $s = 1$, so its sign gives the
class and its value gives the shape $a$. Once $a$ is known, $\kappa_2$ gives
$N$. `log_cumulants_theory()` returns the closed forms, which are polygamma
functions of $a$.

```{r ratio, fig.cap = "Absolute log-cumulant ratio |kappa_3 / kappa_2| as a function of the shape a. The two classes have opposite signs, and for s = 1 the ratio stays below 2 zeta(3) / zeta(2), about 1.46 (dotted line)."}
a <- exp(seq(log(0.05), log(50), length.out = 200))
rho <- function(a, s) { k <- log_cumulants_theory(a, s, r_max = 3); k[2] / k[1] }
r_half <- sapply(a, rho, s = 0.5)
r_one  <- sapply(a, rho, s = 1)
c(range_s_half = range(r_half), range_s_one = range(r_one))
par_default()
plot(a, abs(r_half), log = "xy", type = "l", lwd = 2, col = pal[1],
     xlab = "shape a", ylab = expression("|" * kappa[3] / kappa[2] * "|"),
     ylim = range(abs(c(r_half, r_one))))
lines(a, r_one, lwd = 2, col = pal[2], lty = 2)
abline(h = 2 * 1.2020569 / (pi^2 / 6), lty = 3, col = "grey40")
legend("bottomleft", lwd = 2, col = pal[1:2], lty = 1:2, bty = "n",
       legend = c("s = 1/2 (ratio < 0)", "s = 1 (ratio > 0)"))
```

## Estimating the depth from a sample

`empirical_log_cumulants()` computes $\hat\kappa_2$ and $\hat\kappa_3$ from
a sample of $T_N$, and `fit_homogeneous()` inverts the closed forms. Here the
data come from a cascade with $N = 3$ and $a = 2$; the intermediate levels are
never observed.

```{r fit}
set.seed(2)
T <- sample_TN(c(2, 2, 2), s = 0.5, size = 1e5)
k_hat <- empirical_log_cumulants(T, r_max = 3)
k_true <- log_cumulants_theory(c(2, 2, 2), s = 0.5, r_max = 3)
data.frame(cumulant = c("kappa_2", "kappa_3"), sample = k_hat, theory = k_true)
str(fit_homogeneous(k_hat[1], k_hat[2], s = 0.5))
```

The estimator is consistent, but its spread depends on the sample size. The
next plot repeats the fit on 300 independent samples at each size.

```{r sampling, fig.cap = "Sampling distribution of the depth estimate for a true depth N = 3 (s = 1/2, a = 2), over 300 samples of each size. The dashed line marks the true depth."}
set.seed(3)
N_hat <- sapply(c(1000, 10000), function(n) replicate(300, {
  k <- empirical_log_cumulants(sample_TN(c(2, 2, 2), s = 0.5, size = n), r_max = 3)
  fit <- tryCatch(fit_homogeneous(k[1], k[2], s = 0.5), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(fit)) NA else fit$N
}))
colnames(N_hat) <- c("n = 1000", "n = 10000")
apply(N_hat, 2, quantile, probs = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE)
par_default()
boxplot(N_hat, col = paste0(pal[1:2], "55"), border = pal[1:2],
        ylab = expression(hat(N)), outline = FALSE)
abline(h = 3, lty = 2)
```

## Testing a fixed depth

`test_depth()` is a parametric-bootstrap test of $H_0\colon N = N_0$. With
$n = 1000$ draws from a two-level cascade, the test of $N_0 = 1$ rejects; with
draws from a one-level cascade, it does not. The manuscript measures the size
and power of this test in a simulation study (see [Results of the manuscript](results.html#simulation-size-and-power-of-the-depth-test)).

```{r test}
set.seed(4)
two_levels <- sample_TN(c(2, 2), s = 0.5, size = 1000)
one_level  <- sample_TN(2, s = 0.5, size = 1000)
rbind(true_N_2 = unlist(test_depth(two_levels, N0 = 1, s = 0.5, n_boot = 200)),
      true_N_1 = unlist(test_depth(one_level,  N0 = 1, s = 0.5, n_boot = 200)))
```

## The same argument for networks

In the hierarchical mixed-Poisson model, each vertex has a propensity $W_v$
that is the product of factors attached to its nested communities, and its
degree is Poisson with mean $\lambda W_v$. Mixed-Poisson laws are identifiable
from the degrees, and the factorial moments $\mathrm{E}[D^{(k)}] =
\lambda^k\,\mathrm{E}[W^k]$ carry the log-cumulants of $W$. The depth can
therefore be read from the degree sequence alone.

```{r degrees, fig.cap = "Complementary cumulative degree distribution P(D >= k) of 10^5 simulated vertices for depths N = 0 to 3 (s = 1/2, a = 2, lambda = 20). At equal lambda and a, depth spreads the degrees."}
set.seed(5)
D <- lapply(0:3, function(N) sample_degrees(rep(2, N), s = 0.5, lam = 20, size = 1e5))
par_default()
plot(NULL, xlim = c(1, max(unlist(D))), ylim = c(1e-5, 1), log = "xy",
     xlab = "degree k", ylab = expression(P(D >= k)))
for (i in 1:4) {
  k <- sort(unique(D[[i]]))
  ccdf <- 1 - ecdf(D[[i]])(k - 1)
  lines(pmax(k, 1), ccdf, col = pal[i], lwd = 2, lty = i)
}
legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", col = pal[1:4], lty = 1:4, lwd = 2,
       legend = sprintf("N = %d, VMR = %.1f", 0:3,
                        sapply(D, function(d) var(d) / mean(d))))
```

```{r netfit}
set.seed(6)
D3 <- sample_degrees(c(3, 3, 3), s = 0.5, lam = 15, size = 1e5)
net_fit <- fit_homogeneous_network(D3, s = 0.5)
str(net_fit)
```

The rounded depth is `r net_fit$N_round`, against a true depth $N = 3$, and no
community membership was observed. The point estimates
($\hat N = `r signif(net_fit$N, 3)`$, $\hat a = `r signif(net_fit$a, 3)`$ against
$a = 3$) are less precise than those obtained from $T_N$ itself above, because
the degrees observe $W$ only through Poisson noise. The page *Results of the manuscript*
applies the same estimator to real networks and to turbulence data.
